{{Short description|Theorem in extremal set theory}}
In [[extremal set theory]], the '''Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem''' generalizes the [[Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem]] to {{mvar|t}}-intersecting families. Given parameters {{mvar|n}}, {{mvar|k}} and {{mvar|t}}, it describes the maximum size of a {{mvar|t}}-intersecting family of subsets of <math>\{1,\dots,n\}</math> of size {{mvar|k}}, as well as the families achieving the maximum size.

== Statement ==

Let <math>n \ge k \ge t \ge 1</math> be [[integer]] parameters. A ''{{mvar|t}}-intersecting family'' {{tmath|\cal F}} is a collection of subsets of <math>\{1,\dots,n\}</math> of size {{mvar|k}} such that if {{tmath|A,B \in \cal F}} then <math>|A\cap B| \ge t</math>. [[Péter Frankl|Frankl]]<ref name="auto2">{{harvtxt|Frankl|1978}}</ref>
constructed the {{mvar|t}}-intersecting families

:<math>
\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,r} = \{ A \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\} : |A|=k \text{ and } |A \cap \{1,\dots,t+2r\}| \ge t+r \}.
</math>

The Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem states that if {{tmath|\cal F}} is {{mvar|t}}-intersecting then

:<math>
|\cal F| \leq \max_{r\colon t+2r \leq n} |\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,r}|.
</math>

Furthermore, equality is possible only if {{tmath|\cal F}} is ''equivalent'' to a Frankl family, meaning that it coincides with one after permuting the coordinates.

More explicitly, if

:<math>
(k-t+1)(2+\tfrac{t-1}{r+1}) < n < (k-t+1)(2+\tfrac{t-1}{r})
</math>

(where the upper bound is ignored when <math>r=0</math>)
then <math>|\mathcal{F}| \leq |\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,r}|</math>, with equality if an only if {{tmath|\cal F}} is equivalent to <math>\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,r}</math>; and if

:<math>
(k-t+1)(2+\tfrac{t-1}{r+1}) = n
</math>

then <math>|\mathcal{F}| \leq |\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,r}| = |\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,r+1}|</math>, with equality if an only if {{tmath|\cal F}} is equivalent to <math>\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,r}</math> or to <math>\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,r+1}</math>.

== History ==

Erdős, Ko and Rado<ref>{{harvtxt|Erdős|Ko|Rado|1961}}</ref> showed that if <math>n \ge t + (k-t) \binom{k}{t}^2</math> then the maximum size of a {{mvar|t}}-intersecting family is <math>|\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,0}| = \binom{n-t}{k-t}</math>. Frankl<ref name="auto2"/> proved that when <math>t \ge 15</math>, the same bound holds for all <math>n \ge (t+1)(k-t-1)</math>, which is tight due to the example <math>\mathcal{F}_{n,k,t,1}</math>. This was extended to all {{mvar|t}} (using completely different techniques) by Wilson.<ref name="auto">{{harvtxt|Wilson|1984}}</ref>

As for smaller {{mvar|n}}, Erdős, Ko and Rado made the ''{{tmath|4m}} conjecture'', which states that when <math>(n,k,t)=(4m,2m,2)</math>, the maximum size of a {{mvar|t}}-intersecting family is<ref>{{harvtxt|Erdős|1987|page=56}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Deza|Frankl|1983}}</ref>

:<math>
|\{ A \subseteq \{1,\ldots,4m\} : |A|=2m \text{ and } |A \cap \{1,\ldots,2m\}| \ge m+1 \}|,
</math>
which coincides with the size of the Frankl family <math>\mathcal{F}_{4m,2m,2,m-1}</math>. This conjecture is a special case of the Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem.

Ahlswede and Khachatrian proved their theorem in two different ways: using generating sets<ref name="auto3">{{harvtxt|Ahlswede|Khachatrian|1997}}</ref> and using its dual.<ref name="auto4">{{harvtxt|Ahlswede|Khachatrian|1999}}</ref> Using similar techniques, they later proved the corresponding Hilton–Milner theorem, which determines the maximum size of a {{mvar|t}}-intersecting family with the additional condition that no element is contained in all sets of the family.<ref>{{harvtxt|Ahlswede|Khachatrian|1996}}</ref>

== Related results ==

=== Weighted version ===

[[Gyula O. H. Katona|Katona]]'s intersection theorem<ref>{{harvtxt|Katona|1964}}</ref> determines the maximum size of an intersecting family of subsets of <math>\{1,\dots,n\}</math>. When {{tmath|n=2m+1}} is odd, the unique optimal family consists of all sets of size at least {{tmath|m+1}} (corresponding to the [[Majority function]]), and when {{tmath|n=2m}} is odd, the unique optimal families consist of all sets whose intersection with a fixed set of size {{tmath|2m-1}} is at least {{tmath|m-1}} (Majority on {{tmath|2m-1}} coordinates).

Friedgut<ref>{{harvtxt|Friedgut|2008}}</ref> considered a measure-theoretic generalization of Katona's theorem, in which instead of maximizing the size of the intersecting family, we maximize its {{tmath|\mu_p}}-measure, where {{tmath|\mu_p}} is given by the formula

:<math>
\mu_p(S) = p^{|S|} (1-p)^{n-|S|}.
</math>

The measure {{tmath|\mu_p}} corresponds to the process which chooses a random subset of <math>\{1,\dots,n\}</math> by adding each element with probability {{mvar|p}} independently.

Katona's intersection theorem is the case {{tmath|p=1/2}}. Friedgut considered the case {{tmath|p<1/2}}. The weighted analog of the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem<ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|Frankl|Freed|Lagarias|1986}}</ref> states that if {{tmath|\cal F}} is intersecting then {{tmath|\mu_p(\cal F) \leq p}} for all {{tmath|p < 1/2}}, with equality if and only if {{tmath|\cal F}} consists of all sets containing a fixed point. Friedgut proved the analog of Wilson's result<ref name="auto"/> in this setting: if {{tmath|\cal F}} is {{mvar|t}}-intersecting then {{tmath|\mu_p(\cal F) \leq p^t}} for all {{tmath|p < 1/(t+1)}}, with equality if and only if {{tmath|\cal F}} consists of all sets containing {{mvar|t}} fixed points. Friedgut's techniques are similar to Wilson's.

[[Irit Dinur|Dinur]] and [[Shmuel Safra|Safra]]<ref>{{harvtxt|Dinur|Safra|2005}}</ref> and Ahlswede and Khachatrian<ref name="auto1">{{harvtxt|Ahlswede|Khachatrian|1998}}</ref> observed that the Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem implies its own weighted version, for all {{tmath|p < 1/2}}. To state the weighted version, we first define the analogs of the Frankl families:

:<math>
\mathcal{F}_{n,t,r} = \{ A \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\} : |A \cap \{1,\dots,t+2r\}| \ge t+r \}.
</math>

The weighted Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem states that if {{tmath|\cal F}} is {{mvar|t}}-intersecting then for all {{tmath|0 < p < 1}},

:<math>
\mu_p(\mathcal{F}) \leq \max_{r\colon t+2r \leq n} \mu_p(\mathcal{F}_{n,t,r}),
</math>

with equality only if {{tmath|\cal F}} is equivalent to a Frankl family. Explicitly, <math>\mathcal{F}_{n,t,r}</math> is optimal in the range

:<math>
\frac{r}{t+2r-1} \leq p \leq \frac{r+1}{t+2r+1}.
</math>

The argument of Dinur and Safra proves this result for all {{tmath|p<1/2}}, without the characterization of the optimal cases. The main idea is that if we take a random subset of <math>\{1,\dots,N\}</math> of size {{tmath|\lfloor pN \rfloor}}, then the distribution of its intersection with <math>\{1,\ldots,n\}</math> tends to {{tmath|\mu_p}} as {{tmath|N\to\infty}}.

Filmus<ref>{{harvtxt|Filmus|2017}}</ref> proved weighted Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem for all {{tmath|n,t,p}} using the original arguments of Ahlswede and Khachatrian<ref name="auto3"/><ref name="auto4"/> for {{tmath|p<1/2}}, and using a different argument of Ahlswede and Khachatrian, originally used to provide an alternative proof of Katona's theorem, for {{tmath|p\ge1/2}}.<ref>{{harvtxt|Ahlswede|Khachatrian|2004}}</ref> He also showed that the Frankl families are the unique optimal families for all {{tmath|n,t,p}}.

=== Version for strings ===

Ahlswede and Khachatrian proved a version of the Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem for strings over a finite alphabet.<ref name="auto1"/> Given a finite alphabet {{tmath|\Sigma}}, a collection of strings of length {{mvar|n}} is ''{{mvar|t}}-intersecting'' if any two strings in the collection agree in at least {{mvar|t}} places. The analogs of the Frankl family in this setting are

:<math>
\mathcal{F}_{n,t,r} = \{ w \in \Sigma^n : |w \cap w_0| \ge t+r \},
</math>
where {{tmath|w_0 \in \Sigma^n}} is an arbitrary word, and <math>|w \cap w_0|</math> is the number of positions in which {{mvar|w}} and {{tmath|w_0}} agree.

The Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem for strings states that if {{tmath|\cal F}} is {{mvar|t}}-intersecting then

:<math>
|\mathcal{F}| \leq \max_{r\colon t+2r \leq n} |\mathcal{F}_{n,t,r}|,
</math>

with equality if and only if {{tmath|\cal F}} is equivalent to a Frankl family.

The theorem is proved by a reduction to the weighted Ahlswede–Khachatrian theorem, with <math>p=1/|\Sigma|</math>.
